“Stupid Clanker”: Mediating Racial Discourse Through Robophobia

Nathan Arnold Rothenbaum; Rawan Hegazy; Inna Van Emburg; Kexi Chen

This paper examines the “Clanker” trend, a viral meme that envisions a future wherein artificial intelligence (AI) is the victim of social exclusion and discrimination. Although the trend presents itself as a comedic way to cope with mounting anxieties about AI, we argue that it mobilizes robophobia as a flexible medium for both rehearsing and resisting racist ideologies. Instructional Beliefs Model Meets Task Value: What Role Do Instructor Behaviors and Student Perceptions Play?

Michelle T. Violanti; Stephanie Kelly; Jenilee Croucher Williams; Diyako Rahmani; Samia Powell

The purpose of this study was to examine the factors impacting students’ task value, the utility and future applicability they see in what they are studying/learning in a particular class. Over 375 undergraduate students participated in the online survey study, where they completed scales about instructor clarity, instructor-student rapport, perceived immediacy, information flow, self-efficacy, and task value. Testing the Theory of Motivated Information Management in Online Dating

Ningyang Ocean Wang; Kellie St.Cyr Brisini

Online dating introduces communicative affordances that heighten uncertainty in early relational stages. Guided by the Theory of Motivated Information Management (TMIM), this study examines how individuals manage uncertainty through emotions, efficacy evaluations, and information-seeking behaviors.
